questions.q: Why is batch materialization recommended as the default pattern rather than streaming?
options: Batch materialization requires no scheduling infrastructure at all
Streaming is always technically impossible to build
Most feature freshness requirements are measured in minutes to hours, not seconds, so batch is simpler to operate and sufficient for most features
Streaming ingestion cannot write to any online store
questions.explain: Batch materialization is simpler to build and operate, and it's correct for most features because most freshness needs don't actually require sub-minute data.

questions.q: What specific new risk does the streaming ingestion pattern introduce?
options: It eliminates the possibility of training/serving skew
It makes the offline store obsolete
It removes the need for an online store entirely
A second code path (the stream processor) computes the feature value, which can drift from the training-time logic and reintroduce skew
questions.explain: Streaming ingestion bypasses batch materialization with a separate stream-processing code path, which is a second place feature logic can diverge from the training-time definition — a skew risk.

questions.q: What kind of feature is a good candidate for an on-demand feature view?
options: A feature with no dependencies on any request data
A feature that only needs to be refreshed once a day
A feature that depends on data only known at request time, such as the user's current GPS coordinates
A feature that never changes for any entity
questions.explain: On-demand feature views exist for features that can't be precomputed because they depend on request-time inputs, like live GPS coordinates passed in with the prediction request.

questions.q: Why must an on-demand feature view's transformation logic match the training-time logic exactly?
options: Because it runs on every live request, and if training used different logic for the same feature, that reintroduces the training/serving skew problem feature stores exist to prevent
It doesn't need to match; any transformation logic works equally well
Because on-demand features are never used in training
Because Feast automatically synchronizes any mismatched logic
questions.explain: If the request-time transformation differs from the logic used when building training data, the exact two-code-paths skew problem from Lesson 5 reappears, just inside the on-demand pattern instead of a separate batch/serving split.

questions.q: How should a team decide which architecture pattern to use?
options: Pick exactly one pattern and apply it uniformly to every feature in the project
Always use streaming ingestion for every feature regardless of need
Never use more than one pattern across an entire company
Decide per feature, based on that feature's actual freshness and data-availability requirement — most features on batch, some on streaming, some on-demand
questions.explain: A real feature store typically runs all three patterns side by side, chosen feature by feature based on each feature's actual requirement rather than one architecture applied uniformly.
